newsitem.title: ZAIRE: DEMOCRATIC REPUBLIC OF CONGO - Political temperature rises in Kabila's Congo.
newsitem.headline: DEMOCRATIC REPUBLIC OF CONGO - Political temperature rises in Kabila's Congo.

text.p: Self-declared President Laurent Kabila began his second working week at the helm of Africa's third largest nation on Monday with a political showdown with veteran opposition leader Etienne Tshisekedi brewing.

Kinshasa, capital of Kabila's new Democratic Republic of Congo, went to work normally despite opposition predictions of a stay-home protest and threats of fresh opposition protest marches later in the week.
Shops and offices opened and the teeming city's main market bustled. Witnesses said traffic on the main boulevards, where students protested against Kabila on Friday and Saturday, was normal.

But mutual recriminations between the rivals proliferated over the weekend, with Kabila's administration accusing opposition militants of being impatient and saying it needed time to manage things responsibly.

Kabila's ministers accuse Tshisekedi of deluding the people to feed his own ambition. Tshisekedi aides say Kabila has flooded the capital with foreign troops and accuse him of seeking to return to a one-party state.
"We are seeing a campaign by certain of our compatriots who take pleasure in trying by all means to discredit us," Information Minister Raphael Ghenda told journalists late on Sunday.

Posts and Telecommunications Minister Kinkela Vikansi lambasted Tshisekedi on Monday, accusing him of preaching "xenophobia and racial hatred" and of offering supporters of ousted dictator Mobutu Sese Seko a rallying point.
"He is spreading completely false notions which are disorienting the people," he told Radio France International, adding that he risked becoming "an enemy of the people".
Monday's newspapers in Kinshasa, where Tshisekedi enjoys a significant and often vocal popular following, highlighted the political divide.

Opposition activists say they remain open to dialogue but Tshisekedi aide Laurent Mbayo dismissed as "speculation" a report in the newspaper Le Palmares that the veteran leader had been offered the post of vice-president.
Tshisekedi, citing a 1992 vote in a sovereign national conference in what was then Zaire, has doggedly insisted over the years that constitutionally he is prime minister.
Kabila aides say there will be no post of prime minister in the new administration but Kabila plans to name new ministers to increase the size of his government from 13 to 20.

Opposition activists denounce the presence of Rwandan, Ugandan, Burundian, Angolan and other foreign troops among Kabila's forces. They say they want political dialogue and the departure of foreign troops and threaten to march in the streets of the capital on Wednesday and Friday.
Ghenda told Reuters on Sunday that even if there was initial backing for such protests it was unlikely to last as the people wanted life to return to normal.

Kabila's Alliance of Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Congo marched into Kinshasa on May 17 to crown a seven-month civil war with victory. They took up arms in a dispute over denial of Zairean nationality for ethnic Tutsis.

Ghenda said people calling protests were impatient. "They should give us the time to manage the situation in a responsible manner," he added. "Those behind this kind of action are motivated by their selfish interest."
Kabila's administration has acknowledged security is a problem in the capital and urged the public to help in dealing with the problem.
Kabila said on Saturday that elections, a key demand of the United Nations and many Western nations, would have to wait for two years.
